description: How and where a start-up sells, plus the five lifecycle stages and extension strategies.
content_html:
How Does a Start-Up Reach Its Customers?

Once a business has developed its product, it must decide how customers will be able to buy it. These routes to the customer are called selling channels. Choosing the right channel shapes the price, the customer experience and the cost structure of the business — so it is one of the most practical decisions a new entrepreneur makes.

Broadly speaking, selling channels split into two types: physical channels and digital channels. A start-up may use just one or a combination of both.

Physical Selling Channels

Physical channels involve the customer and the seller meeting in person or collecting the product from a fixed location. Common physical channels for a small start-up include:

  • A shop or market stall — the entrepreneur rents or owns a space where customers can browse and buy. This suits products customers want to touch or try before buying, such as handmade jewellery or fresh produce.
  • Face-to-face selling — visiting customers directly, as a mobile hairdresser or a trades person would. The personal relationship can build loyalty, but it is time-intensive and limits how many customers can be reached.

Physical channels tend to have higher overhead costs (rent, staff, fixtures) but can create a stronger customer experience, particularly where trust or personal service matters.

Digital Selling Channels

Digital channels allow a business to sell to customers anywhere, at any time, without the overhead of a physical premises. For many new start-ups, digital channels are the most affordable way to reach a large audience quickly. Key digital channels include:

E-commerce through a business’s own website gives the entrepreneur full control over branding, pricing and the customer experience. Running costs are lower than a physical shop, and the business can serve customers 24 hours a day. The challenge for a new start-up is driving traffic to the site — without an established reputation, customers may not find it.

Social media platforms now include built-in shopping features where sellers can list and sell products directly to followers. This is a fast, low-cost way for a new business to reach an audience that already follows the brand. Online auction platforms allow businesses to reach a wider audience by listing items in a competitive bidding environment, which can be useful when selling unique or limited-run products. Both routes give access to an existing pool of buyers without requiring the business to build its own customer base from scratch.

Some businesses sell products that exist entirely online — music files, software, digital art, e-books or online courses. These can be delivered instantly to the customer with no physical handling costs, no postage and no stock to manage. Profit margins on digital downloads are typically very high once the product has been created, because the same product can be sold to thousands of customers with no additional production cost.

Key Fact

Physical channels (shop, market stall, face-to-face) suit products that customers want to handle or where personal service matters. Digital channels (e-commerce website, social media marketplace, online auctions, downloads) reduce overheads and extend geographic reach. Most start-ups combine both to maximise sales opportunities.

The Product Lifecycle

Every product, from the day it is conceived to the day it is withdrawn from sale, passes through a series of recognisable stages. This pattern is called the product lifecycle. Understanding which stage a product is at helps a business decide how to price it, how much to spend on promotion, and whether to invest in keeping it alive or launch something new.

The five stages are: development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Sales data tells the story — in an exam, you may be asked to look at a table or graph of sales figures and identify which stage a product is in. You will not be asked to draw the lifecycle curve itself.

During development, the product does not yet exist in a form ready for sale. The business is spending money on research, design and testing but earning nothing. Cash flow is negative and the risk is high — the product may never reach the market.

At introduction, the product launches. Sales begin but are usually low because awareness is limited. Promotional spend is high to build recognition. The business is still likely to be making a loss at this stage. Imagine Floret Skincare, a new Leeds-based soap brand launching its first range — it has costs (ingredients, packaging, marketing) but its first sales are modest.

In the growth stage, sales rise rapidly as the product becomes better known. The business moves into profit. Competitors begin to notice and may enter the market with similar products. Floret Skincare would be expanding its stockists and launching new scents.

At maturity, sales reach their peak and stabilise. This is typically the most profitable stage — most customers in the target market know about the product and competition is fierce. Businesses compete on quality, price and promotion rather than novelty. Branded everyday items like well-known shampoo ranges or breakfast cereals spend years in maturity.

Sales fall consistently during decline. This may happen because consumer tastes change, new technology makes the product obsolete, or a stronger competitor takes market share. A DVD rental service is a well-known example of a business whose core product went into decline as streaming overtook it. At this point the business must decide: withdraw the product, cut costs to serve a small loyal niche, or invest in an extension strategy.

Key Fact

The five stages of the product lifecycle are: development (no sales, spending on creation), introduction (low sales, high promotion, likely a loss), growth (rising sales, rising profit), maturity (peak sales, maximum profit, heavy competition) and decline (falling sales and profit). In an exam, use the shape of sales data to identify the stage.

Extension Strategies

A business rarely wants to withdraw a product once it has built a loyal customer base. Extension strategies are deliberately planned actions to extend the life of a product. They are typically applied during maturity (to prevent decline) or at the start of decline (to reverse it). Common extension strategies include:

  • Increased advertising — a fresh campaign targets existing customers or reaches a new audience, rebuilding awareness and demand.
  • Price reductions — lowering the price attracts customers who were previously put off by the cost, expanding the pool of buyers.
  • Adding value — including extra features, a longer warranty, or bundling with a complementary product makes the offer more attractive without fundamentally redesigning it.
  • New packaging — a refreshed look modernises the product’s appearance without changing what is inside, attracting customers who had lost interest.
  • Entering new markets — selling to a different customer group (younger buyers, a different income segment) or expanding geographically into overseas markets can unlock entirely new revenue streams.

Extension strategies cost money, so the entrepreneur must weigh whether the likely boost in revenue is worth the investment. If the product is genuinely obsolete — no longer wanted by any segment — even a large promotional budget will not revive it. However, for a product with genuine appeal, a well-timed strategy can add years of profitable sales and delay the need to develop something entirely new.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Explain question about selling channels, avoid describing just one channel. Explain why a specific channel suits the start-up in the question — for example, linking a social media marketplace to a young target audience or low start-up budget. That application is what lifts an answer from Developing to Secure. For questions about the product lifecycle, use the sales data provided to name the stage first, then analyse what that stage means for the business’s decisions (pricing, promotion, investment). The examiner’s top complaint is generic answers that could apply to any business. This lesson feeds directly into extended-response evaluation questions on the marketing mix, which account for a significant share of the written exam — practise linking channel choice and lifecycle stage to the full marketing mix.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Selling channels are how a business reaches its customers — physical channels (shops, face-to-face) suit personal or tactile products; digital channels (e-commerce, social media, downloads) reduce costs and extend reach.
  • The five product lifecycle stages are development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Each stage has a different sales level, profitability and set of marketing priorities. In an exam you identify the stage from sales data — you will not be asked to draw the curve.
  • Extension strategies — increased advertising, price reductions, adding value, new packaging and entering new markets — can delay or reverse decline, but only if the cost is justified by the expected boost in revenue.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a digital selling channel?
A) A market stall at a town centre
B) A face-to-face appointment at a customer's home
C) A listing on a social media marketplace
D) A pop-up shop in a shopping centre
practice_questions.marks: C) A listing on a social media marketplace [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two extension strategies a business could use to slow the decline of a product.
practice_questions.marks:
Accept any two of the following (1 mark for the first correct answer — question is 1 mark; accept any single correct extension strategy):
• Increased advertising
• Price reduction
• Adding value (e.g. extra features, longer warranty)
• New packaging
• Entering new markets / geographic expansion
[1 mark for any one clearly stated extension strategy]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to sales and profit during the maturity stage of the product lifecycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each correct point, up to 2 marks:
• Sales have peaked and are stable (or: sales are at their highest level) [1 mark]
• Profit is typically at its maximum, but competition is intense and profit per unit may start to fall [1 mark]
[Both points required for 2 marks; 1 mark if only one is given]

practice_questions.text:
Greystone Press is a small independent publisher based in Sheffield, run by two partners. It sells illustrated books for children. The business is considering adding a digital channel to complement its current face-to-face sales at craft fairs.

Explain one benefit to Greystone Press of selling its books through an e-commerce website.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a point, development and contextual link:
• An e-commerce website would allow Greystone Press to sell books 24 hours a day to customers anywhere in the UK (1 mark), so it is not limited to the visitors who attend the craft fairs it currently relies on (1 mark), meaning revenue is not restricted to fair opening hours and the business could reach families across the country who would never visit Sheffield in person (1 mark).
[1 mark for a valid benefit; 1 mark for development; 1 mark for a contextual link to Greystone Press, craft fairs, or the illustrated children’s book market]

practice_questions.text:
Bramble & Slate is a small homeware brand run by founder Nadia from her workshop in Bath. She sells hand-thrown pottery mugs. Sales data over four years is shown below:
Year 1: 400 units sold | Year 2: 1,800 units sold | Year 3: 3,200 units sold | Year 4: 3,100 units sold

Analyse how the stage of the product lifecycle that Bramble & Slate is currently in might affect Nadia's marketing decisions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Student correctly identifies maturity from the sales data (rising steeply, now plateauing) and makes two or more developed analytical points linking the stage to specific marketing decisions. Uses contextual details (pottery mugs, hand-thrown, Nadia, Bath workshop) throughout. Analysis shows awareness that competition is intensifying and that Nadia must defend market share through promotion or differentiation rather than relying on novelty.

Secure (3-4 marks): Correctly identifies maturity or late growth and links the lifecycle stage to at least one marketing decision with some development. Some use of context from the scenario.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies a lifecycle stage (possibly incorrectly as growth) and makes a basic point about marketing. Little or no use of the scenario details.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic recall of the product lifecycle or a generic marketing statement with no analytical development.

practice_questions.text:
Bramble & Slate's sales have begun to slow. Nadia is deciding between two extension strategies:
Option A: Spend £2,000 on a social media advertising campaign targeting new customers aged 25-40.
Option B: Launch a new gift-set packaging range, selling the existing mugs in pairs with a gift box, at a higher price point.

Justify which option you would recommend to Nadia.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A clear recommendation is made and justified using specific contextual details (hand-thrown pottery, £2,000 budget, gift market, Bath workshop). The student develops a case for the chosen option, addresses a key drawback and explains why the drawback is manageable. The conclusion adds evaluative thinking rather than restating earlier points.

Secure (3-4 marks): A recommendation is made with developed reasoning using some contextual detail. One drawback of the chosen option is acknowledged.

Developing (2 marks): A preference is stated with some reasoning, but analysis is general and context is used only superficially.

Emerging (1 mark): A preference is stated with limited or no reasoning.

knowledge_checks.q: Which stage of the product lifecycle typically generates the highest level of profit?
Which of the following is a digital selling channel?
options: A pop-up shop at a market

knowledge_checks.q: The five stages of the product lifecycle are development, introduction, growth, maturity and _____.
Actions taken by a business to slow or reverse the decline of a product are called _____ strategies.
Match each product lifecycle stage to its key characteristic:
right: No sales yet; the business is spending on research and testing
Sales are falling; the business considers withdrawal or an extension strategy
The product launches; sales are low and promotional costs are high

flashcard_questions.a: The route through which a business makes its product available for customers to buy.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a physical selling channel.
flashcard_questions.a: A shop, market stall or face-to-face appointment.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a digital selling channel.
flashcard_questions.a: An e-commerce website, social media marketplace or online auction.
Buying and selling goods or services electronically, typically through a website.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the five stages of the product lifecycle in order?
Name the product lifecycle stage when sales typically peak.
During which stage does a product usually make a loss?
flashcard_questions.a: Development and introduction — costs exceed revenue from low or zero sales.

flashcard_questions.q: What triggers the decline stage of the product lifecycle?
flashcard_questions.a: Changing consumer tastes, new technology, or stronger competitor products.
An action taken to slow or reverse a product's decline and extend its profitable life.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one extension strategy a business can use when sales start to fall.
flashcard_questions.a: Increased advertising to rebuild awareness and demand.

flashcard_questions.q: How does entering new markets work as an extension strategy?
flashcard_questions.a: Selling to a different customer group or expanding geographically to find new buyers.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might digital downloads have high profit margins for a start-up?
flashcard_questions.a: The same product is sold many times with no additional production cost once created.

flashcard_questions.q: In an exam, how do you identify a product's lifecycle stage?
flashcard_questions.a: By analysing the shape and direction of the sales data provided.

glossary_terms.definition: The routes through which a business makes its product or service available for customers to buy.
Routes through which a business sells directly to customers in a physical location, such as a shop, market stall or face-to-face appointment.
Routes through which a business makes its product or service available to customers online, without requiring a physical meeting point.
Buying and selling goods or services electronically, typically through a website or app.
A model showing the five stages a product passes through from development to decline: development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline.
Actions taken by a business to slow or reverse the decline of a product and boost sales back towards their maturity-stage level.
